hero.caption: On Sunday, February 5, 1865, at Gardner's Gallery in Washington DC, Alexander Gardner took several multiple-lens pictures of the President. Before this session ended, Gardner asked the president for one last pose. He moved his camera closer and took a photograph of Lincoln’s head, shoulders, and chest.  Mysteriously the glass plate negative cracked. Gardner carefully took it to his dark room and was able to make one print, with an ominous crack across Lincoln’s face, before it broke completely and was discarded. This print, known as O-118, still exists to this day. Over the years many people have associated this crack with a symbolic foretelling of the assassin’s bullet that awaited Lincoln 10 weeks later.

images.filename: Gibbs-Coolidge Collection - 1817 to 1821 - by Gilbert Stuart - National Gallery of Art, Washington DC.jpg
images.caption: Oil on wood portraits of Presidents George Washington, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and James Monroe by Gilbert Stuart, circa 1817 to 1821. Stuart painted the five presidents as part of a set commissioned by Colonel George Gibbs of Rhode Island. These were some of the last paintings in Stuart's career. Much later, the Gibbs family sold the set to Thomas Jefferson Coolidge, an ancestor of President Calvin Coolidge. The Coolidge family sold the five portraits (known as the Gibbs-Coolidge Collection) to the National Gallery of Art in April 1979.
images.alt: Oil on wood portraits of Presidents George Washington, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and James Monroe by Gilbert Stuart, circa 1817 to 1821. Two 65 ft-long strands of lightbulbs are hung vertically between the tall columns on the ornate facade of the Old Patent Office Building. images.caption: Picture of one portion of Félix González-Torres's text portrait artwork "Untitled" (1989) at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C., in 2025, installed as part of the exhibition Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Always To Return. A close-up image of text painted on a wall near the ceiling, directly below the crown molding at the top of the wall. The text, painted in silver, reads "Trump Medieval Bold Italic 1956", a reference to the specific font the artist used for his text portrait artworks. The phrase is one part of a larger date portrait made by the artist and modified by the curators; this phrase was added to this iteration of the work by the curators.

images.caption: Picture of a detail from Félix González-Torres's artwork "Untitled" (Portrait of Robert Vifian) (1993) at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C., in 2025, as part of the exhibition Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Always To Return. The phrase "First T.V. 1966" is painted in silver italic font on a wall near the ceiling, just below the decorative molding at the top of the wall. The phrase is one part of a larger date portrait made by the artist and modified by the curators. This phrase was included in the first iteration of the work created by the artist.
